value.overview: The Green-fronted Lancebill (Doryfera ludovicae) is a large, distinctive hummingbird of humid mountain forests in Central and South America. Its most obvious features are an exceptionally long, straight bill and a bright green forehead. It commonly lives near rushing streams, forested ravines, and waterfalls, where it visits long tubular flowers. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of wet highland forests, especially along the Caribbean side of the central mountain ranges, but it is generally uncommon and local.
value.classification: The Green-fronted Lancebill belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Doryfera. Two subspecies are commonly recognized, including Doryfera ludovicae veraguensis, which occurs in Costa Rica and western Panama.
value.identification: This is a relatively large hummingbird with a very long, slender, straight bill. Adults have a glittering green forehead, mostly dusky or grayish underparts, and green to bronzy-green upperparts. The tail is dark, often with pale or whitish tips visible in flight. Its combination of long bill, green frontal patch, and preference for shaded stream corridors helps separate it from other Costa Rican hummingbirds. It is usually seen singly or in concealed perches near flowers and water.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a discontinuous range extending from Costa Rica and western Panama south through the Andes of Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in humid montane and premontane forests of the central and southern highlands, particularly on the Caribbean slope from the Cordillera de Tilarán southward. It favors forest canopy, edges, ravines, and streamside vegetation, usually near rushing water or waterfalls, at roughly 750 to 2,800 meters elevation.
value.migrationStatus: The Green-fronted Lancebill is considered resident in Costa Rica. It is not a regular long-distance migrant, although individuals may make local or seasonal movements in response to flowering and weather conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information is less extensively documented than for many common hummingbirds. In Costa Rica, nesting is associated with humid montane forest, ravines, and stream corridors. The female is responsible for nest construction, incubation, and care of the young, while the male may defend feeding territories and display or sing from perches. The nest is a small cup, typically placed in sheltered vegetation near a stream or other moist forest habitat.
value.dietFeeding: The Green-fronted Lancebill feeds mainly on nectar from long, tubular flowers, especially epiphytic plants in the heath family and other flowers whose shape suits its unusually long bill. It also takes small arthropods, providing protein for adults and growing young. It often forages in the canopy, along forest edges, and beside streams, and may defend productive flower patches from other hummingbirds.
value.behavior: This hummingbird is usually inconspicuous and spends much of its time perched quietly in shaded forest. Males may gather in loose groups or defend territories around flowering plants, sometimes giving characteristic songs from exposed perches. Females tend to forage and travel more along ravines and streams. Young birds may descend into shrubs, clearings, and forest edges to use shorter-tubed flowers. Flight is rapid and maneuverable, especially around streamside vegetation and waterfalls.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified, but the species is generally regarded as broadly distributed with no confirmed rapid decline.
